::: {.reading-meta}
12 minute read · Pilot data, methodology, and code at [github.com/Yazidryuichi/biomarker-iium-pipeline](https://github.com/Yazidryuichi/biomarker-iium-pipeline)
:::

::: {.first-letter}

In an Indonesian primary school, a child sits in front of a laptop with fifteen wet electrodes on her scalp. She closes her eyes during a resting-state recording. Somewhere on the recording laptop, a Python script is logging her EEG at 250 Hz. Twenty-seven other children, ages six to twelve, contributed to the same dataset.

:::

The data she produced has been analysed by every clinical EEG textbook for the last forty years. The textbooks all agree on what an executive-function biomarker is supposed to look like. They are wrong, at least about her cohort.

Forty years of theta/beta-ratio literature has not invented its findings. What it has done is collapse a rich multidimensional signal into a single ratio and, over generations of replication, taught itself that the ratio is the signal. It isn't. The ratio is one projection of a much larger object, and the rest of that object carries information the field has been systematically throwing away.

The methodological move that recovered the signal is borrowed from a place neuroscience does not usually shop. The mathematical object is called a density matrix. Physicists know it as the standard tool for representing a quantum system in a mixed state. The same object can be constructed directly from EEG, with no quantum hardware in the loop, by averaging unit-normalized analytic signals across channels and time. Section 3 builds it from the data.

The next twelve minutes walk through the pilot, show what the textbook biomarker did and did not do, and report a comparison on the same twenty-eight children. A linear classifier on the entries of the density matrix reaches mean balanced accuracy [0.657]{.num-chip} and ROC AUC [0.780]{.num-chip} under repeated stratified 10-fold cross-validation. The best classical QEEG classifier on the same children, same folds, reaches [0.618]{.num-chip} and [0.615]{.num-chip}. The AUC gap is [0.165]{.num-chip} on a single cohort, and it comes from an exploratory analysis rather than a confirmatory test.

::: {.figure-caption}
**Figure 0.** A 4-second loop showing fifteen 10-20-system electrodes appearing on a child's scalp during the impedance check. Cohort: N = 28 children, ages 6-12, recorded at Islamic Green School, Indonesia. Pipeline: HAPPE → ICA → average reference. Sampling rate 250 Hz.
:::
